KP25 Boosting and AdaBoost: Turning Weak into Strong

One-sentence summary: A classifier only a little better than guessing, retrained again and again on the samples it got wrong and combined by a weighted vote, can push the training error as low as you like; but boosting is no panacea.

1. Weak to strong

Plain explanation: Can a weak classifier be boosted into a strong one? (Labels y∈{±1}y\in\{\pm1\}y∈{±1} and classifier outputs ϕ∈{±1}\phi\in\{\pm1\}ϕ∈{±1}.)

  • Weak classifier: one whose error is only a little better than guessing (0.5).
  • Stump: a tree that asks one question about one feature, such as "xj>0x_j>0xj​>0?".

Example (designed here): two 20-D Gaussians (means ∓a\mp a∓a, a=2/20a=2/\sqrt{20}a=2/20​), 200 training, 400 test points; the 20 stumps "xj>0x_j>0xj​>0?" err 27% to 36%, mean 31.6%. The mechanism: reweight the samples every round, giving hard (misclassified) points more weight, then take a weighted vote.

Figure lec05-kp25-weak: the test errors of the 20 stumps.

2. Where weights come from

Stage-wise optimization: optimize only the newly added classifier and freeze the earlier ones: Fm=Fm−1+αmϕmF_m=F_{m-1}+\alpha_m\phi_mFm​=Fm−1​+αm​ϕm​. Split stage by stage, the exponential loss (KP20) ∑iexp⁡(−yiF(xi))\sum_i\exp(-y_iF(x_i))∑i​exp(−yi​F(xi​)) becomes

J=∑iwiexp⁡(−yiαϕ(xi)),wi=exp⁡(−yiFm−1(xi)). J=\sum_iw_i\exp\big(-y_i\alpha\phi(x_i)\big),\qquad w_i=\exp\big(-y_iF_{m-1}(x_i)\big). J=i∑​wi​exp(−yi​αϕ(xi​)),wi​=exp(−yi​Fm−1​(xi​)).

wiw_iwi​ contains neither α\alphaα nor ϕ\phiϕ, so it is the sample weight; ϕm\phi_mϕm​ then minimizes the weighted error PmP_mPm​ (weights normalized to sum 1).

Figure lec05-kp25-wts: the weights emerge from the exponential loss.

3. The voice α

Formal definition: back in JJJ, αm=arg⁡min⁡{e−α(1−Pm)+eαPm}\alpha_m=\arg\min\{e^{-\alpha}(1-P_m)+e^{\alpha}P_m\}αm​=argmin{e−α(1−Pm​)+eαPm​} and a zero derivative gives

αm=12ln⁡1−PmPm. \alpha_m=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1-P_m}{P_m}. αm​=21​lnPm​1−Pm​​.

P=0.1P=0.1P=0.1: 1.099; 0.3: 0.424; 0.5: 0; 0.7: −0.424-0.424−0.424. Accurate → a large voice; guessing → 0; worse than guessing (P>0.5P>0.5P>0.5) → negative, use its answer inverted.

Figure lec05-kp25-alpha: α\alphaα against the weighted error.

5. The algorithm

wi=1/Nw_i=1/Nwi​=1/N; repeat: find ϕm\phi_mϕm​ minimizing PmP_mPm​, compute αm\alpha_mαm​, update and normalize the weights; finally f(x)=sign⁡∑kαkϕk(x)f(x)=\operatorname{sign}\sum_k\alpha_k\phi_k(x)f(x)=sign∑k​αk​ϕk​(x). Setup (Example 4.3 redone here): two 20-D Gaussians, 200 training and 400 test points; each round picks the best stump over all features and thresholds; 2000 rounds. Round 1: training error 25.5% and test error 28.75%, better than an arbitrary fixed stump (mean 31.6%).

Figure lec05-kp25-algo: the AdaBoost algorithm.

6. The error curves

Training error: 25.5% at round 1, 4.5% at round 10 and 0 from round 17 on. Test error: 28.75% (1), 12.25% (10), 4.75% (50), 3.25% (200), 4.0% (500), 4.25% (2000). After the training error reaches zero the test error keeps falling, then stays near 4% after about 200 rounds, flat within sampling error (with 400 test points 1% is only 4 points).

Figure lec05-kp25-curve: training and test error against rounds (log axis).

7. The margin explanation

Normalized margin margin⁡=yF(x)/∑kαk∈[−1,1]\operatorname{margin}=yF(x)/\sum_k\alpha_k\in[-1,1]margin=yF(x)/∑k​αk​∈[−1,1]: positive only if correct, larger means more confidence. The bound (Schapire et al.): generalization error ≲prob⁡{margin⁡<γ}+O(Vc/(Nγ2))\lesssim\operatorname{prob}\{\operatorname{margin}<\gamma\}+O(\sqrt{V_c/(N\gamma^2)})≲prob{margin<γ}+O(Vc​/(Nγ2)​), independent of the number of rounds KKK; this is the source of the immunity. Experiment (designed here), smallest margin: −1.000-1.000−1.000 at round 1, −0.205-0.205−0.205 at 10, +0.148+0.148+0.148 at 50, +0.203+0.203+0.203 at 200, +0.220+0.220+0.220 at 2000; share with margin <0.1<0.1<0.1: 25.5%, 8.5%, 0%. The criticism: the bound is very loose (unless NNN is in the tens of thousands) and only a qualitative explanation; stage-wise optimization is itself an implicit regularization.

Figure lec05-kp25-margin: the smallest margin and test error at different rounds.

8. No panacea

Example (designed here): data of the same kind with 15% of the training labels flipped at random; means of 5 fresh draws for 0% and 15% (so unlike the single run before; test labels are clean). Test error: clean: 14.4% (10 rounds) → 6.6% (100) → 5.5% (2000); 15% flipped: 19.1% → 18.9% → 23.3%, lowest 17.8% (30 rounds). A likely cause: the exponential loss punishes bad samples with large negative margins too much; after 2000 rounds the 15.5% flipped samples hold 36% of the weight (one run). Common misconception: AdaBoost never overfits; on hard tasks with a high Bayes error and noisy labels it can degrade sharply (source). To remember: weak classifiers + weighting the points that are wrong + a weighted vote; the weights fall out of the exponential loss and α\alphaα is set by the weighted error.

Figure lec05-kp25-noise: test error with clean labels and with 15% flipped.

(2) The wrong one 0.2×2=0.40.2\times2=0.40.2×2=0.4 and each of the 4 right ones 0.2×0.5=0.10.2\times0.5=0.10.2×0.5=0.1; Z=0.8Z=0.8Z=0.8; normalized: 0.5 for the wrong one and 0.125 for each right one.
